$$\begin{aligned} & \text { So, } \tan 45^{\circ}=\left|\frac{2-m_2}{1+2 m_2}\right| \\ & \Rightarrow \quad 1=\left|\frac{2-m_2}{1+2 m_2}\right| \\ & \Rightarrow 1+2 m_2=2-m_2 \text { or } 1+2 m_2=-\left(2-m_2\right) \\ & 2 m_2+m_2=2-1 \text { or } 1+2 m_2=-2+m_2 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad 3 m_2=1 \quad \Rightarrow 2 m_2-m_2=-2-1 \\ & \therefore m_2=\frac{1}{3}, m_2=-3 \end{aligned}$$

en.content: If 2 and 3 are intercepts of a line L = 0, then the distance of L $$\equiv$$ 0 from the origin is
en.explanation:

$$\begin{array}{ll} \Rightarrow & \frac{x}{2}+\frac{y}{3}=1 \\ \Rightarrow & 3 x+2 y-6=0 \end{array}$$

$$=\left|\frac{3(0)+2(0)-6}{\sqrt{3^2+2^2}}\right|=\frac{|-6|}{\sqrt{13}}=\frac{6}{\sqrt{13}}$$

en.content: How many 5-digit numbers greater than 50,000 can be formed using the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 without repetition?
en.explanation:
Total number formed by using 5 digits $=\frac{5 !}{2 !}$

$$ =\frac{5 \times 4 \times 3 \times 2 !}{2 !}=60 $$

For number greater than 50,000 , digit 2 cannot come at first place.

Hence, number formed in which 2 is at the first place

$$ =\frac{4 !}{2 !}=\frac{4 \times 3 \times 2 !}{2 !}=12 $$

Hence, total number formed greater than 50000

$$ =60-12=48 $$

en.content: If kinetic energy of a body is increased by 300%, then percentage change in momentum will be
en.explanation:
As,

$$K=\frac{1}{2} m v^2$$

$$\Rightarrow \quad K=\frac{1}{2 m} p^2$$

$$\Rightarrow \quad p^2=2 m K$$

$$\Rightarrow \quad p=\sqrt{2 m K}$$

Suppose, $$p_1$$ is the momentum of the body and $$K_1$$ = kinetic energy of the body initially. As the kinetic enery of the body is increased by $$300 \%$$, new kinetic energy of the body $$=K_1+3 K_1$$

Hence, percentage change in momentum

$$\begin{aligned} & =\frac{p_2-p_1}{p_1} \times 100 \\ & =\frac{\sqrt{2 m K_2}-\sqrt{2 m K_1}}{\sqrt{2 m K_1}} \times 100 \\ & =\frac{\sqrt{2 m} \sqrt{K_2}-\sqrt{K_1}}{\sqrt{2 m} \sqrt{K_1}} \times 100 \\ & =\frac{\sqrt{K_1+3 K_1}-\sqrt{K_1}}{\sqrt{K_1}} \times 100 \\ & =\frac{\sqrt{4 K_1}-\sqrt{K_1}}{\sqrt{K_1}} \times 100=100 \% \end{aligned}$$

en.content: Which of the following diagram represents the variation of the electric field with distance r from the centre of a uniformly charged non-conducting sphere of radius R?

$$\begin{aligned} & E=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{q}{R^2} \\ \Rightarrow & E \propto \frac{1}{R^2} \end{aligned}$$

where, $$R$$ being the radius of sphere.

The electric field intensity inside the sphere is

$$\begin{array}{ll} \Rightarrow & E=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{q r}{R^3} \\ \Rightarrow & E \propto r \end{array}$$

At the centre of sphere, $$E=0$$

Hence, option (c) is correct representation.

en.content: A DC ammeter and a hot wire ammeter are connected to a circuit in series. When a direct current is passed through circuit, the DC ammeter shows 6 A. When AC current flows through circuit, what is the average readings in DC ammeter and the AC ammeter, if DC and AC currents flows simultaneously through the circuit?
en.explanation:
Resultant current is superposition of two currents, i.e. $$I$$ (instantaneous total current)

$$=6+I_0 \sin \omega t$$

$$\mathrm{DC}$$ ammeter will read average value

$$\begin{aligned} & =\overline{6+I_0 \sin \omega t}\\ & =6 \mathrm{~A} \end{aligned}$$

$$\left(\because \overline{I_0 \sin \omega t}=0\right)$$

$$\mathrm{AC}$$ ammeter will read average value

$$\begin{aligned} & =\sqrt{\overline{\left(6+I_0 \sin ^2 \omega t\right)^2}} \\ & =\sqrt{36+12 I_0 \sin \omega t+I_0^2 \sin ^2 \omega t}\end{aligned}$$

$$\left(\because \overline{I_0 \sin \omega t}=0\right)$$

Since, $$\overline{\sin ^2 \omega t}=\frac{1}{2}$$ and $$I_{\mathrm{rms}}=8=\frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \therefore \mathrm{AC} \text { reading }=\sqrt{36+\frac{I_0^2}{2}} & =\sqrt{36+64} \\ & =10 \mathrm{~A}\end{aligned}$$

en.content: A bullet of mass $m$ hits a mass $$M$$ and gets embedded in it. If the block rises to a height $$h$$ as a result of this collision, the velocity of the bullet before collision is
en.explanation:
Let the velocity of the bullet before collision be $$v$$, then according to law of conservation of linear momentum,

$$m v=(m+M) v^{\prime}$$ ..... (i)

As the mass $m$ of the bullet gets embedded in the wall, hence velocity of bullet + target just after collision will be same,

$$\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{2}(M+m) v^{\prime 2}=(m+M) g h \\ & \Rightarrow \quad v^{\prime}=\sqrt{2 g h} \\ \end{aligned}$$

Putting the value of $$v^{\prime}$$ in Eq. (i), we get

$$\Rightarrow \quad v=\sqrt{2 g h} \frac{(m+M)}{m}=\sqrt{2 g h}\left(1+\frac{M}{m}\right)$$

en.content: A particle of mass $$m$$ is moving in a horizontal circle of radius $$r$$ under a centripetal force given by $$\left(\frac{-K}{r^2}\right)$$, where $$K$$ is a constant. Then

options.content: the total energy of the particle is $$\left(\frac{-K}{2 r}\right)$$
the kinetic energy of the particle is $$\left(\frac{K}{r}\right)$$
the potential energy of the particle is $$\left(\frac{K}{2 r}\right)$$
the kinetic energy of the particle is $$\left(\frac{-K}{r}\right)$$

en.explanation:
The potential energy is given by

$$\begin{aligned} U & =\int F \cdot d r=\int \frac{K}{r^2} d r=K \int r^{-2} d r \\ & =K\left[\frac{r^{-1}}{-1}\right]=\frac{-K}{r} \end{aligned}$$

The kinetic energy is given by

$$K=\frac{1}{2} m v^2=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{K}{r}\right) \quad\left[\because \frac{m v^2}{r}=\frac{K}{r^2}\right]$$

Total energy, $$E=U+K$$

$$=\frac{-K}{r}+\frac{K}{2r}=\frac{-K}{2r}$$

en.content: The height at which the acceleration due to gravity becomes $$\frac{g}{16}$$ (where, g = acceleration due to gravity on the surface of the earth) in terms of R is, if R is the radius of earth.

en.content: The wavelength of the second line of Balmer series is 486.4 nm. What is the wavelength of the first line of Lyman series?
en.explanation:
Wavelength in Balmer series for hydrogen are given by

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{\lambda} & =R_{\mathrm{H}}\left(\frac{1}{2^2}-\frac{1}{n^2}\right) \\ & =R_{\mathrm{H}}\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{n^2}\right), n=3,4,5, \ldots \end{aligned}$$

The second line in Balmer series corresponds to $$n=4$$

Hence, $$\frac{1}{\lambda_2}=R_{\mathrm{H}}\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{16}\right)=\frac{3 R_{\mathrm{H}}}{16}$$

or, $$\lambda_2=\frac{16}{3 R_{\mathrm{H}}}$$

The wavelength of the first line $$(n=2)$$ in Lyman series is

$$\begin{array} & \frac{1}{\lambda_1}=R_{\mathrm{H}}\left(1-\frac{1}{2^2}\right)=R_{\mathrm{H}}\left(1-\frac{1}{4}\right)=\frac{3 R_{\mathrm{H}}}{4} \\ \text { or, } \quad \lambda_1=\frac{4}{3 R_{\mathrm{H}}} \\ \therefore \quad \frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}=\frac{4}{3 R_{\mathrm{H}}} \times \frac{3 R_{\mathrm{H}}}{16}=\frac{1}{4} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \lambda_1=\frac{\lambda_2}{4}=\frac{486.4}{4}=121.6 \mathrm{~nm} \end{array}$$

en.content: A disc of moment of inertia 4 kg - m$$^2$$ revolving with 16 rad/s is placed on another disc of moment of inertia 8 kg - m$$^2$$ revolving 4 rad/s. The angular frequency of composite disc
en.explanation:

en.content: Television frequencies are of the order of 100 MHz, while radio frequencies are of the order of 1 MHz. Using these as typical frequencies, the ratio of the emf generated in a loop antenna by a television wave to that generated by a radio wave, if both have equal electric field intensities.
en.explanation:
As we know that, emf induced $$e=\frac{d \phi_B}{d t}$$

or $$e=\frac{dB}{dt}$$ (when area is constant $$\phi_B \propto B$$)

Now for television wave, $$e_1=\frac{d}{d t}(B)$$

$$\begin{aligned} & =\frac{d}{d t}\left(B_0 \sin \left(2 \pi f_1 t+\phi\right)\right) \\ e_1 & =B_0 2 \pi f_1 \cos \left(2 \pi f_1 t+\phi\right) \end{aligned}$$

For radiowave, $$e_2=\frac{d}{d t}(B)$$

$$\begin{aligned}& =\frac{d}{d t}\left(B_0 \sin \left(2 \pi f_2 t+\phi\right)\right) \\ = & B_0 2 \pi f_2 \cos \left(2 \pi f_2+\phi\right) \end{aligned}$$

The ratio of emf induced

$$=\frac{e_1}{e_2}=\frac{B_0 2 \pi f_1 \cos \left(2 \pi f_1 t+\phi\right)}{B_0 2 \pi f_2 \cos \left(2 \pi f_2 t+\phi\right)}$$

Since, $$f_1=100 \mathrm{MHz}, f_2=1 \mathrm{MHz}$$ and $$\cos \left(2 \pi f_1 t+\phi\right)=\cos \left(2 \pi f_2 t+\phi\right)=\cos \phi$$ (For complete cycle)

We get, $$\frac{e_1}{e_2}=\frac{100}{1}=100$$

en.content: A particle is performing simple harmonic motion. Equation of its motion is $$x = 5\sin \left( {4t - {\pi \over 6}} \right),x$$ being the displacement from mean position. Velocity (in ms$$^{-1}$$) of the particle at the instant when its displacement is 3, will be

en.content: A galvanometer having a resistance of 4 $$\Omega$$ is shunted by a wire of resistance 2 $$\Omega$$. If the total current is 1.5 A, the current passing through shunt is
en.explanation:

en.content: In Young's double slit experiment, the two slits are separated by 0.2 mm and they are 1 m from the screen. The wavelength of the light used is 500 nm. The distance between 6th maxima and 10th minima on the screen is closest to

en.content: A series L-C-R circuit is connected to an AC source of 220 V and 50 Hz shown in figure. If the readings of the three voltmeters $$V_1,V_2$$ and $$V_3$$ are 65 V, 415 V and 204 V respectively, the value of inductance and capacitance will be

en.explanation:
The capacitance of a conductor is defined as the ratio of the charge given to the rise in the potential of the conductor.

$$\begin{aligned} & C=\frac{q}{V}=\frac{q^2}{W} \quad\left(V=\frac{W}{q}\right) \\ & C=\frac{\text { ampere }^2-\text { second }^2}{\mathrm{~kg}^2-\text { metre }^2 \text { second }^{-2}} \end{aligned}$$

Hence, dimensionally $$\left[\mathrm{M}^{-1} \mathrm{~L}^{-2} \mathrm{~T}^4 \mathrm{~A}^2\right]$$

From Ohm's law, $$V=I R$$,

Hence,

$$\begin{aligned} R & =\frac{V}{I}=\frac{\text { Volt }}{\text { Ampere }}=\frac{W}{q} \times \frac{t}{q} \\ R & =\frac{F \times s \times t}{q^2}=\mathrm{kg} \frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}^2} \times \frac{\mathrm{m} \times \mathrm{s}}{\mathrm{A}^2 \times \mathrm{s}^2} \\ & =\mathrm{kg} \mathrm{m}^2 \mathrm{~s}^{-3} \mathrm{~A}^{-2} \end{aligned}$$

Dimensionally, $$R=\left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-3} \mathrm{~A}^{-2}\right]$$

Hence,

$$\begin{aligned} C R & =\left[\mathrm{M}^{-1} \mathrm{~L}^{-2} \mathrm{~T}^4 \mathrm{~A}^2\right]\left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-3} \mathrm{~A}^{-2}\right] \\ & =\left[\mathrm{M}^0 \mathrm{~L}^0 \mathrm{~T}\right] \end{aligned}$$

en.content: An ideal gas is taken through the cycle A $$\to$$ B $$\to$$ C $$\to$$ A, as shown in the figure. If the net heat supplied to the gas in the cycle is 5 J, the work done by the gas in the process C $$\to$$ A is,
en.explanation:
Net work done by a gas,

$$\begin{array}{ll} \Delta W_{A B}=p \cdot \Delta V=10 \times(2-1)=10 \mathrm{~J} \\ \Delta W_{B C}=0 & \text { (as } V=\text { constant) } \end{array}$$

From first law of thermodynamics, we have,

$$\begin{aligned}\Delta Q & =\Delta W+\Delta U \\ \Delta U & =0 \end{aligned}$$

(process $$A B C A$$ is cyclic)

Therefore, $$\Delta Q=\Delta W_{A B}+\Delta W_{B C}+\Delta W_{C A}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad \Delta W_{C A} & =\left(\Delta Q-W_{A B}-W_{B C}\right) \\ & =(5-10-0) \mathrm{J}=-5 \mathrm{~J} \end{aligned}$$

en.content: From a circular disc of radius R, a square is cut out with a radius as its diagonal. The centre of mass of remaining portion is at a distance (from the centre)
en.explanation:
Radius of the circular disc $$=R$$

Suppose, centre of mass of remaining portion is at a distance $$C_2$$ from the centre $$C$$.

Now, $$A_1\left(C C_1\right)=A_2\left(C C_2\right)$$

$$\therefore CC_2=\frac{A_1}{A_2}(CC_2)$$

For square, $$(\text { side })^2+(\text { side })^2=(\text { radius })^2$$

$$\begin{array}{r} 2(\text { side })^2=R^2 \\ (\text { side })^2=\frac{R^2}{2} \\ \text { side }=\frac{R}{\sqrt{2}} \end{array}$$

Now, $$A_1\left(C C_1\right)=A_2\left(C C_2\right)$$

$$A_1=$$ area of the square $$=\left(\frac{R}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2$$

$$A_2=$$ area of the remaining part of the circle

$$=\pi R^2-\left(\frac{R}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2$$

$$\begin{aligned} C C_2 & =\frac{\left(\frac{R}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2}{\pi R^2-\left(\frac{R}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2}\left(\frac{R}{2}\right) \\ & =\frac{R^2}{2\left(\pi R^2-\frac{R^2}{2}\right)} \cdot \frac{R}{2} \\ & =\frac{R^2}{2 \pi R^2-R^2} \cdot \frac{R}{2} \\ & =\frac{R \cdot R \cdot R}{R^2(2 \pi-1) 2}=\frac{R}{4 \pi-2}\end{aligned}$$

en.content: A bar magnet of length $$6 \mathrm{~cm}$$, is placed in the magnetic meridian with $$N$$ pole, pointing towards the geographical north. Two neutral points, separated by a distance of $$8 \mathrm{~cm}$$ are obtained on the equitorial axis of the magnet. If $$B_H=1.2 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~T}$$. Then the pole strength of the magnet is

A force F applied on the wire of radius r and length L and change in the length of the wire is $$l$$. If the same force F is applied on the wire of the same material and radius 4r and length $$4l$$, then change in length of the other wire is,
en.explanation:
As per formula, the Young's modulus, $$\mathrm{Y=\frac{Stress}{Strain}}$$

$$ = {{{F \over A}} \over {{{\Delta l} \over l}}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow F = {{YA\Delta l} \over l}$$

In first case, $$Y = {{{F \over {{A_1}}}} \over {{{{l_1}} \over L}}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow F = {{Y{l_1}{A_1}} \over L}$$ ...... (i)

Similarly, for the second case,

$$F = {{Y{l_2}{A_2}} \over {\Delta l}}$$ ...... (ii)

From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get

$${{Y{l_1}{A_1}} \over L} = {{Y{l_2}{A_2}} \over {4L}}$$

As Y is same, as the same material is taken, $${l_1}{A_1} = {{{l_2}{A_2}} \over 4}$$

$${l_1}\pi {r^2} = {{{l_2}} \over 4}\pi {(4r)^2}$$

$${l_1} = {{{l_2}} \over 4}\,.\,{{16{r^2}} \over {{r^2}}} = 4{l_2} \Rightarrow {l_2} = {{{l_1}} \over 4}$$

Here, $${l_1} = l,{l_2} = {l \over 4}$$

en.content: Two guns P and Q can fire bullets at speeds 2 km/s and 4 km/s, respectively. From a point on a horizontal ground, they are fired in all possible directions. The ratio of maximum or areas covered by the bullets fired by the two guns, on the ground is
en.explanation:
As for the projectile motion, horizontal range,

$$R = {{{u^2}\sin 2\theta } \over g}$$

$$\because$$ Maximum range $$ = {u^2}/g$$

$$\because$$ $$A = \pi {R^2}$$

$$\therefore$$ $$A \propto {R^2}$$

i.e., $$A \propto {u^4}$$

$$\therefore$$ $${{{A_1}} \over {{A_2}}} = {{u_1^4} \over {u_2^4}} = {\left( {{2 \over 4}} \right)^4} = {\left( {{1 \over 2}} \right)^4} = {1 \over {16}}$$

en.content: A cell of emf 2 V is connected with a load of resistance 1.5 $$\Omega$$. The power delivered by the cell to the load is maximum, then power transferred to the load is
en.explanation:
Given, emf of cell, $$E=2V$$

Load resistance, $$R_L=1.5~\Omega$$

Current flowing the circuit is

$$I=\frac{E}{R+r}$$

Power transferred to the load, R,

$$P = {I^2}R = {\left( {{E \over {R + r}}} \right)^2}\,.\,R = {{{E^2}R} \over {{{(R + r)}^2}}}$$

Power P will be maximum, if

$$dP/dR = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow {d \over {dR}}{{{E^2}R} \over {{{(R + r)}^2}}} = 0$$

$$ \begin{array}{ll} \Rightarrow & \frac{E^2(R+r)^2-E^2 \cdot R \cdot 2(R+r)}{(R+r)^3}=0 \\ \Rightarrow & E^2(R+r)[R+r-2 R]=0 \\ \Rightarrow & E^2(R+r)(r-R)=0 \\ \Rightarrow & r-R=0 \\ \Rightarrow & r=R \end{array}$$

$$\therefore$$ Maximum power, $$P=\frac{E^2 R}{(R+r)^2}=\frac{E^2 R}{(R+R)^2}=\frac{E^2}{4 R}$$

$$\Rightarrow \quad P=\frac{2^2}{4 \times 1.5}=\frac{1}{3}=0.33 \mathrm{~W}$$

en.content: A plane glass mirror of thickness 3 cm of material of $$\mu=\frac{3}{2}$$ is silvered on the black surface. When a point object is placed 9 cm from the front surface of the mirror, then the position of the brightest image from the front surface is
en.explanation:
A thick glass mirror produces a number of images. There is an apparent shift of actual silvered surface towards the unsilvered face.

Effective distance of the reflecting surface from unsilvered face $$=\frac{d}{\mu}$$

$$\frac{3}{3/2}$$ cm = 2cm

Distance of point object from effective reflecting surface = 9 cm + 2 cm = 11 cm

Distance of image from point object

= 11 cm + 11 cm = 22 cm

Distance of image from unsilvered face

= (22 $$-$$ 9) cm = 13 cm

en.content: Ultraviolet light of wavelength 99 mm falls on a metal plate of work function 1.0 eV. If the mass of the electron is 9.1 $$\times$$ 10$$^{-31}$$ kg, the wavelength of the fastest photoelectron emitted is
en.explanation:

$$\begin{aligned} & K_{\max }=h v-W_0 \\ & =\frac{\left(6.6 \times 10^{-34}\right) \times\left(3 \times 10^8\right)}{99 \times 10^{-9}}-1.0 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \\ & =2 \times 10^{-18}-1.6 \times 10^{-19} \\ & =1.84 \times 10^{-18} \mathrm{~J} \end{aligned}$$

Now,

en.content: There are two identical containers C$$_1$$ and C$$_2$$ containing to identical gases. Gas in C$$_1$$ is reduced to half of its original volume adiabatically, while the gas in container C$$_2$$ is also reduced to half of its initial volume isothermally. Find the ratio of final pressure in these containers. ($$\gamma$$ be the adiabatic constant).
en.explanation:
Since, container are identical, so initial volume and pressure will be same for identical gases.

For container C$$_1$$,

$${p_1}V_1^\gamma = {p_2}V_2^2$$ (adiabatic)

$${p_2} = {\left( {{{{V_1}} \over {{V_2}}}} \right)^\gamma }{p_1} = {\left( {{{{V_1}} \over {{V_1}/2}}} \right)^\gamma }{p_1} = {2^\gamma }{p_1}$$ ..... (i)

For container C$$_2$$,

$${p_1}{V_1} = {p_2}'{V_2}$$ (isothermal)

$${p_2}' = \left( {{{{V_1}} \over {{V_2}}}} \right){p_1} = \left( {{{{V_1}} \over {{V_1}/2}}} \right){p_1} = 2{p_1}$$ ..... (ii)

From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get

$${{{p_2}} \over {{p_2}'}} = {{{2^\gamma }{p_1}} \over {2{p_1}}} = {2^{\gamma - 1}}:1$$

en.content: If K$$_1$$ and K$$_2$$ are maximum kinetic energies of photoelectrons emitted when lights of wavelengths $$\lambda_1$$ and $$\lambda_2$$, respectively incident on a metallic surface and $$\lambda_1=3\lambda_2$$, then
en.explanation:
Let $$W_0$$ be the work function of the metal, then kinetic energy of photoelectrons emitted when light of wavelength $$\lambda_1$$ is incident will be

$$K_1=\frac{h c}{\lambda_1}-W_0$$

Similarly, $$\quad K_2=\frac{h c}{\lambda_2}-W_0$$

$$\begin{aligned}\text { Now, } K_1-K_2 & =\frac{h c}{\lambda_1}-\frac{h c}{\lambda_2}=h c\left[\frac{1}{\lambda_1}-\frac{1}{\lambda_2}\right] \\ & =h c\left[\frac{1}{3 \lambda_2}-\frac{1}{\lambda_2}\right] \\ K_1-K_2 & =\frac{-2 h c}{3 \lambda_2}=\frac{-2}{3}\left(K_2+W_0\right) \\ \Rightarrow \quad K_1 & =K_2-\frac{2}{3} K_2-\frac{2}{3} W_0 \\ & =\frac{K_2}{3}-\frac{2}{3} W_0 \Rightarrow K_1<\frac{K_2}{3}\end{aligned}$$

en.content: A car is moving with a speed of 54 km/h. If after 3 s, the driver applies brakes and it stops, then how much distance is covered by the car before coming to rest?
en.explanation:
Given, speed of car, $$u=54 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{h}=54 \times \frac{5}{18}=15 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$$

Since, car stops in $$3 \mathrm{~s}$$ on applying brakes, so acceleration can be calculated from first equation of motion,

$$\begin{aligned} & \quad v=u+a t \Rightarrow 0=15+a(3) \\ & \Rightarrow \quad a=-\frac{15}{3}=-5 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2} \end{aligned}$$

Using second equation of motion,

$$\begin{aligned} s & =u t+\frac{1}{2} a t^2 \\ & =15 \times 3+\frac{1}{2} \times(-5) \times(3)^2 \\ & =4 5-22.5=22.5 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned}$$

en.content:
A source of sound emits sound waves at frequency $$f_0$$. It is moving towards an observer with fixed speed $${v_s}$$ ($${v_s},v$$, where $$v$$ is the speed of sound in air.) If the observers were to move towards the source with speed $$v_0$$, one of the following two graphs (A and B) will give the correct variation of the frequency $$f$$ heard by the observer as $$v_0$$ is changed.

The variation of $$f$$ with $$v_0$$ is given correctly by
en.explanation:
According to Doppler's effect, the apparent frequency or sound when both source and observer are moving towards each other

$$ \Rightarrow f = {{(v + {v_0}){f_0}} \over {(v - {v_0})}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow f = \left( {{v \over {v - {v_s}}}} \right){f_0} + \left( {{{{v_0}} \over {v - {v_s}}}} \right){f_0}$$

$$ \Rightarrow f = \left( {{{{f_0}} \over {v - {v_s}}}} \right){v_0} + \left( {{{{f_0}} \over {v - {v_s}}}} \right)v$$

Equation of straight line, $$y=mx+c$$ which is equation of straight line making an intercept $$c$$ on Y-axis,

Slope of the graph $$ = {{{f_0}} \over {v - {v_s}}}$$ and intercept $$ = {{v{f_0}} \over {v - {v_s}}}$$

This condition is represented in graph A plotted between $$f$$ and $$v_0$$.

Hence, option (c) is correct.

en.content: The escape velocity of a projectile on the earth's surface is 11.2 km/s. A body is projected out with thrice this speed. The speed of the body far away from the earth will be
en.explanation:
By the law of conservation of energy,

$$\begin{aligned} & (U+K)_{\text {surface }}=(U+K)_{\infty} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \frac{-G M}{R}+\frac{1}{2} m\left(3 v_e\right)^2=0+\frac{1}{2} m v^2 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad-\frac{G M}{R}+\frac{9 v_e^2}{2}=\frac{1}{2} v^2 \\ & \text { Since, } v_e^2=\frac{2 G M}{R} \\ & \therefore \quad \frac{-v_e^2}{2}+\frac{9 v_e^2}{2}=\frac{1}{2} v^2 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad v^2=8 v_e^2 \\ & v=2 \sqrt{2} v_e=2 \sqrt{2} \times 11.2=31.7 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{s} \\ \end{aligned}$$

en.content: With what minimum acceleration can a fireman slide down a rope while breaking strength of the rope is $$\frac{2}{3}$$ of the weight?
en.explanation:
If a man slides down with some acceleration, then its apparent weight decreases. For critical condition, rope can bear only $$\frac{2}{3}$$ of his weight. If a is the minimum acceleration, then tension in the rope

$$=m(g-a)=$$ breaking strength

$$\Rightarrow m(g-a)=\frac{2}{3}mg$$

$$\Rightarrow a=g-\frac{2g}{3}=\frac{g}{3}$$

en.content: The string of length 2 m is fixed at both ends. If the string vibrates in its fourth normal mode with a frequency of 500 Hz, then the waves would travel on it with a velocity of
en.explanation:

Given, $$\nu=500$$ Hz, $$l=2$$ m

Hence, $$500=\frac{4\nu}{2\times2}$$

or, $$v=\frac{500\times4}{4}=500$$ m/s

en.content: Two charged spheres of $$-20\mu$$C and $$60\mu$$C are kept at a certain distance. They are touched and kept again at the same distance. What is the ratio of force experienced before and after?
en.explanation:
Given, $$q_1=-20 \mu \mathrm{C}=-2 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{C}$$

$$q_2=60 \mu \mathrm{C}=6 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{C}$$

Force of attraction between the both charges, kept at a certain distance $$r$$,

$$\begin{aligned} F_1 & =\frac{K q_1 q_2}{r^2} \\ & =\frac{K \times 2 \times 10^{-5} \times 6 \times 10^{-5}}{r^2} \\ & =\frac{12 \times 10^{-10} K}{r^2} \end{aligned}$$

When both charges are touched, then new charge on both spheres,

$$\begin{aligned} q_1^{\prime} & =q_2^{\prime}=\frac{q_1+q_2}{2}=\frac{-20+60}{2}=20 \mu \mathrm{C} \\ & =2 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{C} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore$$ Force between the two spheres,

$$F_2=\frac{K q_1^{\prime} \cdot q_2^{\prime}}{r^2}$$

$$=\frac{K \cdot 2 \times 10^{-5} \times 2 \times 10^{-5}}{r^2}$$

$$=\frac{4 \times 10^{-10}}{r^2} K$$

$$\therefore$$ $${{{F_1}} \over {{F_2}}} = {{{{12 \times {{10}^{ - 10}}K} \over {{r^2}}}} \over {{{4 \times {{10}^{ - 10}}} \over {{r^2}}}}} = {{12} \over 4} = {3 \over 1}$$

$$\therefore$$ $${F_1}:{F_2} = 3:1$$
